questions.question: In birds, the sex of the offspring is decided by
options: the male parent, because males are ZW
the female parent, because females are ZW
the male parent, because males are XY
the female parent, because females are XO

solution.key_concept: Birds follow the ZW-ZZ type of sex determination, with female heterogamety.
steps: In birds, females are ZW and males are ZZ.
Females produce two kinds of eggs, Z-bearing and W-bearing, while all sperms carry Z.
The egg therefore decides the sex, so the mother determines the sex of the offspring.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): the female parent, because females are ZW
solution.why_not_others: Option 1 is wrong because males are ZZ, which makes them homogametic. Option 3 describes the human XY system, not birds. Option 4 describes the XO system of grasshoppers.
solution.common_trap: Students often carry over the human rule that the father determines sex and apply it to birds.

questions.question: A male honey bee (drone) has how many chromosomes in its cells, and by which division does it produce sperms?
options: 32 chromosomes; meiosis
16 chromosomes; mitosis
16 chromosomes; meiosis
32 chromosomes; mitosis

solution.key_concept: Haplodiploid sex determination in the honey bee.
steps: A drone develops from an unfertilised egg by parthenogenesis.
It is therefore haploid, with n = 16 chromosomes.
Because it is already haploid, it produces sperms by mitosis.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): 16 chromosomes; mitosis
solution.why_not_others: 32 is the diploid number found in females (queens and workers). A haploid cell cannot undergo normal meiosis to form gametes, so meiosis is incorrect.
solution.common_trap: Assuming all sperms arise by meiosis.

questions.question: In a grasshopper showing the XO type of sex determination, the somatic cells of a female contain 24 chromosomes. How many chromosomes will the somatic cells of a male contain?

solution.key_concept: In the XO type, males have a single X and therefore one chromosome fewer than females.
steps: Females are XX and have 24 chromosomes.
Males have only one X, with no partner sex chromosome.
Male number = 24 - 1 = 23.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): 23
solution.why_not_others: 24 ignores the missing X. 22 subtracts both X chromosomes. 12 is a haploid count, not a somatic number.
solution.common_trap: Assuming that males and females of a species always have equal chromosome numbers.

questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: In humans, the sex of the child is determined by the father.
statements.R: Human males produce two types of sperms in equal proportion, X-bearing and Y-bearing, while all eggs carry an X chromosome.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Male heterogamety in humans (XX-XY type).
steps: All eggs carry X, so the egg makes no difference to sex.
The sperm carries either X (giving a girl) or Y (giving a boy).
Since the sperm decides the sex, the father determines it. R explains A.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
solution.why_not_others: Both statements are true facts, and R gives the direct cause of A, so options 2, 3 and 4 do not apply.
solution.common_trap: Thinking the mother contributes to sex determination in humans.

questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: A drone honey bee has no father but does have a grandfather.
statements.II: A queen honey bee develops from a fertilised egg, whereas a worker develops from an unfertilised egg.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: In the honey bee, all females are diploid; queen and worker differ only in nutrition.
steps: A drone comes from an unfertilised egg, so it has no father.
Its mother (the queen) had a father, so the drone has a grandfather. Statement I is correct.
Both queen and worker develop from fertilised diploid eggs (2n = 32).
Their difference comes from nutrition (royal jelly), not from fertilisation. Statement II is incorrect.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
solution.why_not_others: Statement II wrongly attributes the queen-worker difference to fertilisation. Only drones arise from unfertilised eggs.
solution.common_trap: Believing workers are haploid or genetically different from queens.

questions.question: Who used recombination frequency as a measure of the distance between genes and constructed the first chromosome maps?
options: Thomas Hunt Morgan
Henking
Alfred Sturtevant
Gregor Mendel

solution.key_concept: Origin of chromosome mapping.
steps: Morgan discovered linkage and coined the terms linkage and recombination.
His student Alfred Sturtevant used recombination frequency as a measure of gene distance.
Using this, Sturtevant constructed the first chromosome maps.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): Alfred Sturtevant
solution.why_not_others: Morgan coined the term linkage but did not make the first maps. Henking described the X body. Mendel did not work on linkage.
solution.common_trap: Crediting Morgan with mapping because he did the Drosophila linkage work.

questions.question: A test cross involving two linked genes produced 500 progeny, of which 60 showed recombinant (non-parental) combinations. What is the distance between the two genes?
options: 88 cM
6 cM
12 cM

solution.key_concept: $RF = \frac{\text{number of recombinants}}{\text{total progeny}} \times 100$, and 1% recombination = 1 cM.
steps: Recombinants = 60 and total progeny = 500.
Since 1% recombination = 1 cM, the distance is 12 cM.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): 12 cM
solution.why_not_others: 88 cM uses the parental count (440) instead of the recombinant count. 13.6 cM divides by the parentals (60/440) instead of the total. 6 cM wrongly halves the frequency.
solution.common_trap: Dividing recombinants by parentals instead of by total progeny.

questions.question: Recombination by crossing over during meiosis occurs
options: at zygotene, between sister chromatids
at pachytene, between non-sister chromatids, mediated by recombinase
at pachytene, between sister chromatids, mediated by ligase
at diplotene, between non-homologous chromosomes

solution.key_concept: Crossing over takes place at pachytene of prophase I.
steps: Crossing over occurs at the pachytene stage of prophase I.
It takes place between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes.
The enzyme recombinase mediates it.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): at pachytene, between non-sister chromatids, mediated by recombinase
solution.why_not_others: Exchange between sister chromatids would produce no new combinations. Zygotene and diplotene are the wrong stages. Ligase is not the enzyme named for crossing over.
solution.common_trap: Confusing pachytene with zygotene (synapsis) or diplotene (chiasmata become visible).

questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: A
list_I.text: Yellow body and white eye genes

list_I.label: B
list_I.text: White eye and miniature wing genes

list_II.label: III
list_II.text: Only parental types in a test cross

options: A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III
A-IV, B-II, C-III, D-I
A-IV, B-II, C-I, D-III
A-I, B-II, C-IV, D-III

solution.key_concept: Recombination frequency reflects the tightness of linkage between genes.
steps: Yellow-white genes are tightly linked and show 1.3% recombination (A-IV).
White-miniature genes are loosely linked and show 37.2% recombination (B-II).
1% recombination equals 1 cM (C-I).
Complete linkage gives only parental types in a test cross (D-III).
solution.final_answer: Option (3): A-IV, B-II, C-I, D-III
solution.why_not_others: Option 1 swaps the tight and loose pairs. Option 2 swaps C and D. Option 4 mismatches A and C.
solution.common_trap: Swapping the yellow-white and white-miniature recombination values.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about linkage and recombination are correct?

statements.A: In Morgan's dihybrid crosses with X-linked genes in Drosophila, F2 ratios deviated strongly from 9:3:3:1.
statements.B: Tightly linked genes show high recombination.
statements.C: Recombination frequency is proportional to the distance between genes.
statements.D: Morgan coined the term linkage for the physical association of genes on a chromosome.
statements.E: In Morgan's crosses, recombinant combinations outnumbered parental combinations.

options: A, C and D only
A, B and C only
C, D and E only
A, C, D and E only

solution.key_concept: Linkage keeps parental combinations together; recombination increases with distance between genes.
steps: A is correct: Morgan's F2 ratios deviated strongly from 9:3:3:1.
B is incorrect: tightly linked genes show low recombination.
C and D are correct statements of fact.
E is incorrect: parental combinations far outnumbered recombinants.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): A, C and D only
solution.why_not_others: Option 2 includes B, which is false. Options 3 and 4 include E, which is false.
solution.common_trap: Associating tight linkage with high recombination.

questions.question: A haemophilic man marries a woman who is neither haemophilic nor a carrier. What is expected among their children?
options: All sons haemophilic and all daughters normal
All daughters carriers and all sons normal
Half the sons haemophilic and half the daughters carriers
All daughters haemophilic and all sons normal

solution.key_concept: An affected father passes his X only to his daughters.
steps: The father gives his X (carrying the haemophilia allele) to every daughter and his Y to every son.
Daughters receive a normal X from the mother as well, so all daughters are carriers.
Sons receive their X from the normal mother, so all sons are normal.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): All daughters carriers and all sons normal
solution.why_not_others: Option 1 wrongly assumes father-to-son transmission. Option 3 is the outcome for a carrier mother and normal father. Option 4 is wrong because daughters also get a normal X from the mother.
solution.common_trap: Assuming an affected father passes an X-linked trait to his son.

questions.question: A woman with normal vision, whose father was colour blind, marries a man with normal vision. What proportion of their sons is expected to be colour blind?

solution.key_concept: A daughter of an affected father is a carrier, and a carrier mother passes the allele to half her sons.
steps: The woman received the colour-blind X from her father, so she is a carrier.
Each son receives one of her two X chromosomes.
Half her sons therefore receive the defective X and are colour blind.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): 50%
solution.why_not_others: 0% ignores her carrier status. 25% is the chance of an affected son among all children, not among sons. 100% would require the mother to be colour blind.
solution.common_trap: Confusing the fraction among sons with the fraction among all children.

questions.question: For a daughter to be born haemophilic, her parents must be
options: a haemophilic father and a mother who is at least a carrier
a normal father and a carrier mother
a haemophilic father and a normal non-carrier mother
a normal father and a haemophilic mother

solution.key_concept: A female needs two recessive X-linked alleles, one from each parent.
steps: A daughter receives one X from each parent.
To be affected, both X chromosomes must carry the haemophilia allele.
So the father must be haemophilic and the mother must be at least a carrier, which is why such females are very rare.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): a haemophilic father and a mother who is at least a carrier
solution.why_not_others: In options 2 and 4 the normal father gives a normal X, so the daughter can only be a carrier. In option 3 the normal mother gives a normal X, so the daughter is again only a carrier.
solution.common_trap: Thinking a carrier mother alone can produce an affected daughter.

questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: Colour blindness occurs in about 8% of males but only about 0.4% of females.
statements.R: Colour blindness results from defects in the red or green cones of the eye.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Sex difference in X-linked recessive traits arises from male hemizygosity.
steps: A is a correct frequency statement.
R correctly describes the cone defect behind colour blindness.
The higher frequency in males is explained by males being hemizygous for the X-linked recessive allele, not by the cone defect. So R does not explain A.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
solution.why_not_others: Both statements are true, which rules out options 3 and 4. R does not explain the male-female difference, which rules out option 1.
solution.common_trap: Choosing option 1 simply because both statements concern colour blindness.

questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: In criss-cross inheritance, an X-linked trait passes directly from an affected father to his son.
statements.II: When a carrier woman marries a normal man, all their daughters are expected to be carriers.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: Criss-cross inheritance and the carrier mother x normal father cross.
steps: Criss-cross inheritance runs from an affected father, through a carrier daughter, to her son. A son never receives his father's X, so Statement I is incorrect.
A carrier mother x normal father gives 50% of daughters as carriers, not all. Statement II is incorrect.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
solution.why_not_others: Each statement contains an error, so no option that marks either one as correct can apply.
solution.common_trap: Mixing up this cross with the affected father x normal mother cross, which does give all daughters as carriers.

questions.question: Thalassemia is inherited as a/an
options: autosomal dominant disorder
autosomal recessive disorder
X-linked recessive disorder
Y-linked disorder

solution.key_concept: Thalassemia is an autosomal recessive Mendelian disorder.
steps: Thalassemia is transmitted when both parents are unaffected carriers.
Unaffected carrier parents producing an affected child is the pattern of a recessive trait.
The genes involved lie on autosomes (chromosomes 16 and 11).
solution.final_answer: Option (2): autosomal recessive disorder
solution.why_not_others: A dominant disorder would show in carriers. The genes lie on chromosomes 16 and 11, not on X or Y.
solution.common_trap: Grouping all blood disorders with haemophilia as X-linked.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the genetic basis of beta thalassemia?
options: A single gene, HBB, on chromosome 11 of each parent, giving two genes in total
Two closely linked genes, HBA1 and HBA2, on chromosome 16 of each parent, giving four genes in total
A single gene, HBB, on chromosome 16 of each parent, giving two genes in total
A single gene, HBB, on chromosome 11 of each parent, giving four genes in total

solution.key_concept: Beta thalassemia involves HBB on chromosome 11; alpha thalassemia involves HBA1 and HBA2 on chromosome 16.
steps: Beta chain production is controlled by the single gene HBB.
HBB lies on chromosome 11.
One copy comes from each parent, giving two genes in total.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): A single gene, HBB, on chromosome 11 of each parent, giving two genes in total
solution.why_not_others: Option 2 describes alpha thalassemia. Option 3 gives the wrong chromosome. Option 4 gives the wrong gene count.
solution.common_trap: Swapping chromosome 16 (alpha) with chromosome 11 (beta).

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes thalassemia from sickle-cell anaemia?
options: Thalassemia is a qualitative defect, while sickle-cell anaemia is a quantitative defect
Both are X-linked recessive disorders of haemoglobin
In thalassemia too few globin chains are synthesised, while in sickle-cell anaemia an incorrectly functioning globin is made
Sickle-cell anaemia results from substitution at the 6th position of the alpha globin chain

solution.key_concept: Thalassemia is a quantitative defect; sickle-cell anaemia is a qualitative defect.
steps: In thalassemia, a mutation or deletion reduces how much of a globin chain is made, which is a quantitative problem.
In sickle-cell anaemia, Glu is replaced by Val at position 6 of the beta chain, producing a faulty globin, which is a qualitative problem.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): In thalassemia too few globin chains are synthesised, while in sickle-cell anaemia an incorrectly functioning globin is made
solution.why_not_others: Option 1 reverses the two terms. Both disorders are autosomal recessive, not X-linked. The sickle-cell substitution is in the beta chain, not the alpha chain.
solution.common_trap: Reversing the qualitative and quantitative labels.

questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_II.label: I
list_II.text: Glu replaced by Val at the 6th position of the beta chain

list_II.label: II
list_II.text: Missing enzyme that converts phenylalanine to tyrosine

list_II.label: III
list_II.text: HBA1 and HBA2 genes on chromosome 16

options: A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV
A-I, B-II, C-IV, D-III
A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV
A-III, B-II, C-I, D-IV

solution.key_concept: The molecular basis of common Mendelian disorders.
steps: Sickle-cell anaemia: GAG becomes GUG, so Glu is replaced by Val at position 6 of the beta chain (A-I).
Phenylketonuria: the enzyme converting phenylalanine to tyrosine is missing (B-II).
Alpha thalassemia: HBA1 and HBA2 on chromosome 16 (C-III).
Beta thalassemia: HBB on chromosome 11 (D-IV).
solution.final_answer: Option (1): A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV
solution.why_not_others: Option 2 swaps the alpha and beta thalassemia genes. Option 3 swaps sickle-cell and phenylketonuria. Option 4 mismatches A and C.
solution.common_trap: Swapping the chromosome 16 and chromosome 11 assignments.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about thalassemia and related Mendelian disorders are correct?

statements.A: Thalassemia is transmitted to offspring when both parents are unaffected carriers.
statements.B: In alpha thalassemia, the more of the four alpha globin genes that are affected, the less alpha globin is produced.
statements.C: Two carrier parents have a 25% chance of having a thalassemic child.
statements.D: Thalassemia is a sex-linked recessive disorder.
statements.E: Phenylketonuria is an autosomal dominant disorder.

options: A, B and C only
A, B, C and D only
B, C and E only
A and C only

solution.key_concept: Thalassemia is autosomal recessive, and alpha thalassemia severity depends on how many genes are affected.
steps: A is correct: carriers transmit the disorder.
B is correct: the more genes affected, the less alpha globin is made.
C is correct: Aa x Aa gives 1/4 aa.
D is incorrect: thalassemia is autosomal. E is incorrect: phenylketonuria is autosomal recessive.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): A, B and C only
solution.why_not_others: Option 2 includes D, which is false. Option 3 includes E, which is false, and omits A. Option 4 omits B, which is true.
solution.common_trap: Labelling every blood disorder as sex-linked, as with haemophilia.
